headline: Cotton holds Arkansas as all 75 counties move toward the Democrats
dek: Tom Cotton won a third term by 11.9 points, compared with Donald Trump's 30.6 in 2024. The biggest shifts came in Northwest Arkansas, Jonesboro and De Queen. The smallest came in the Delta counties that already vote Democratic.
summary: Cotton won by 11.9 points, down from Trump's 30.6; all 75 counties moved left and Washington and Desha flipped.

paras.text: Tom Cotton, the Republican, beat Democrat Hallie Shoffner 480,627 votes to 375,647 on Tuesday with 99 percent of the expected vote counted. His margin was 11.9 points. Two years ago Donald Trump carried Arkansas by 30.6 points over Kamala Harris. The difference of 18.8 points showed up everywhere on the map: all 75 counties moved toward the Democrats, and the typical county moved 16 points.

In the governor's race, Sarah Huckabee Sanders won by 15.3 points over Democratic state Sen. Fred Love of Little Rock, so Shoffner's margin was about three and a half points better than her party's candidate for governor. Neither result ended the streak: Democrats have not won a statewide or U.S. House race in Arkansas since 2010. About 885,800 Senate votes were counted, roughly 75 percent of the 1,182,676 cast for president in 2024. Trump's statewide lead of about 362,000 votes shrank to Cotton's lead of about 105,000.
A farmer's campaign against a well-funded incumbent

Shoffner, 38, is a former rice and soybean farmer. She chose to challenge Cotton after she closed her family's 150-year-old Jackson County soybean farm due to tariffs imposed by the Trump administration, according to the Arkansas Advocate. The Associated Press reported that her campaign focused on how tariffs and rising fuel prices were hurting the state's farmers. The Advocate also reported that disrupted commerce in the Middle East during the war has caused gasoline and fertilizer prices to spike, and Shoffner said that frustration was drawing voters to her.

Cotton, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, and Republican allies had heavily outspent Shoffner in the race, with ads portraying her as soft on immigration and too closely allied with national Democrats. Preelection polling roughly matched the result. A Talk Business & Politics–Hendrix College survey in October found Cotton ahead by 9 percentage points, with only 5% of voters remaining as undecided.

The biggest move among large counties came in Northwest Arkansas. Washington County, home to Fayetteville and Springdale, went from Trump by 6.7 points to Shoffner by 17.5, a 24-point move on 76,041 votes. Next door in Benton County, Trump's 27-point margin shrank to Cotton's 6.1, about 6,000 votes. Two political scientists told the Advocate that Benton County exemplified the party's loosening grip on Arkansas. The shift carried down the ballot. Democrats flipped five House seats in Benton and Washington counties and won an 8-7 majority on the Washington County Quorum Court.

Craighead County, which includes Jonesboro, moved 24 points, from Trump by 37.4 to Cotton by 13.6. There, Democrat Erika Askeland, a third grade public school teacher from Jonesboro, won the House District 32 seat, unseating the six-consecutive-term incumbent, Republican Rep. Jack Ladyman. Mississippi County, in the northeast corner, moved 25 points. Desha County in the Delta flipped, going from Trump by 4.8 to Shoffner by 12.3. Jackson County, where Shoffner grew up, moved 19 points.

The biggest move in the state came in a small county. Sevier County, whose seat is De Queen, went from Trump by 61.7 to Cotton by 30.4, a 31-point move on just 3,098 votes. The 2020 census put the county's Hispanic population at 5,508, or about thirty-five percent of the total county population. Many of those residents moved there for work offered by the poultry companies. The county count cannot say who changed or who stayed home.

The smallest moves came in the places Democrats already held. Jefferson County, which includes Pine Bluff, moved 9 points, from Harris by 20.1 to Shoffner by 29.0. Phillips County moved 10. Pulaski County, which includes Little Rock and had the most votes at 130,223, moved 13 points to a 35.2-point Democratic margin. Two strongly Republican counties in the Ozark foothills, Cleburne and Baxter, each moved about 10 points, among the smallest moves in the state.
Who moved, and what the count cannot tell

Counties are not voters, and the charts beside this section compare places, not people. They point in one direction. The three counties with more than 50,000 votes, which cast 34 percent of the ballots, moved 18.4 points when weighted by votes. The 56 counties with fewer than 10,000 votes moved 15.8. The two counties Trump won by less than 10 points, Washington and Desha, moved 23.9. The 61 counties he won by 30 or more, which cast 59 percent of the vote, moved 16.7. The three counties Harris won by 10 to 30 points moved 12.5.

Turnout tells a similar story. Statewide, 74.9 percent as many votes were cast as in 2024. In the seven counties where turnout held up best, at 80 to 95 percent of the 2024 total, the move was 13.1 points. In the 65 counties in the 65-to-80 percent range, which cast 82 percent of the vote, it was 17.8. The link is weak (a correlation of -0.26), but counties where turnout fell more tended to move more. Jay Barth of Hendrix College told the Advocate that "in some places, especially rural areas, it was a slightly demobilized Republican electorate," while Democrats did better in urban and suburban areas. Washington County shows the limits of a turnout-only explanation. Its turnout, at 78 percent of 2024, was close to the state average, yet it moved 24 points. Still, the county count cannot separate voters who changed their minds from voters who stayed home.

Reports on how many people voted point in different directions. The Advocate reported that about one-third of Arkansas' 1.85 million registered voters cast their ballot ahead of Election Day, more than in the 2022 midterms. An analysis by the University of Arkansas extension service, reported by TriArk Radio, said the election attracted the fewest voters in more than a decade of elections. Those numbers are unofficial.

John Davis of the University of Arkansas said that while other states swung to Democrats, "in Arkansas, we had something of a red wall". Below the statewide races, though, Democrats flipped 11 state legislative districts, the party's biggest gain in the General Assembly in more than two decades. That broke the Republican supermajority in the House. A spokesperson for Sanders said Wednesday that Arkansas remains a very conservative state with large Republican majorities in the Legislature.
